links.note: 411 calls what comes through the ear (செவிச்செல்வம்) the செல்வத்துள் செல்வம், the wealth among wealths. 241 gives the same title, in the same words, to அருட்செல்வம், and adds a reason: material wealth is found even among the base (பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள). The formula is a way of ranking an inner good above goods, and the book uses it twice with different winners, once in the Book of Virtue and once in the Book of Wealth.

400 says learning is the wealth that does not perish (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்) and that other things are not wealth at all (மாடல்ல). 411 makes the matching claim for listening: it is the head of all wealth (செல்வத்துளெல்லாந் தலை). The adjacent chapters on learning and on listening each present their subject as the real wealth, set against possessions.

412 treats listening as food for the ear (செவிக்குணவு) and lets the stomach have a little (சிறிது) only when that food is absent. 420 turns the same ear-and-mouth pairing into a judgment: for those who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear (செவியிற் சுவையுணரா வாயுணர்வின் மாக்கள்), living and dying come to the same. The chapter's ranking of the two appetites starts as a rule for mealtimes and ends as a measure of a life.

412 allows the stomach only a little (சிறிது), and Parimelazhagar explains the word by saying heavy eating multiplies disease and desire. 946, in the chapter on medicine, says well-being stays with the one who eats knowing to stop short (இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்) and disease with the heavy eater (கழிபேர் இரையான்). The same restraint at the table is asked for in the name of listening in one verse and in the name of health in the other.

413 says those who have listening as their ear's food, though on the ground (நிலத்து), are equal to those fulfilled by the food of oblation (அவியுணவின் ஆன்றாரோடொப்பர்), whom Parimelazhagar takes as the gods. 50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived (வையத்துள் வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன்) is placed among the gods. Both verses grant godlike standing to someone still on earth, one for the householder's conduct and one for listening. The word for 'dwelling in the sky' in 50 is misprinted in this edition, but the sense is not in doubt.

413 makes listeners equal to the oblation-fed (ஆன்றாரோடொப்பர்). 702 says one who knows without doubt what is inside another (அகத்தது உணர்வான்) should be taken as equal to a god (தெய்வத்தோடொப்பக் கொளல்). In both, a human being is ranked with the gods for a faculty of taking in what others carry: their teaching in one, their unspoken thought in the other.

414 says: even if you have not studied, listen, and it will be a prop in weakness (ஒற்கத்தின் ஊற்றாந் துணை). 415 repeats the image of the prop (ஊற்றுக்கோல்) on slippery ground but attaches it to a particular source, the words of those who have good conduct (ஒழுக்கமுடையார் வாய்ச்சொல்). Read together, the open invitation to listen is narrowed to a question of whom one listens to; Manakkudavar says outright that 415 is about listening to people of conduct.

403 says even the unlearned are very good if they can keep from speaking before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 414 addresses the same person (கற்றிலனாயினும்) and tells him to listen (கேட்க). The silence that 403 only recommends as damage control becomes in 414 the means of gaining what he lacks.

415 says the words from the mouth of those with conduct (ஒழுக்கமுடையார் வாய்ச்சொல்) are like a staff where the ground is slippery (இழுக்கல் உடையுழி). 139 says of the same people (ஒழுக்கமுடையவர்க்கு) that speaking evil with the mouth, even by a slip (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்), is not possible. 139 gives the reason 415 needs: those who do not slip in what they say are the ones whose words can steady someone who is slipping.

415 presents the words of people of conduct as the staff that keeps a person upright on slippery ground. 447 asks who can ruin a ruler who keeps as his own those who will rebuke him (இடிக்குந் துணையார்). Both verses locate safety in another person's speech; 447 applies it to a king and makes the helpful words explicitly unwelcome ones.

396 says understanding wells up in proportion to learning (கற்றனைத்தூறும் அறிவு), as water in a sand-well comes as far as one digs (தொட்டனைத்து). 416 uses the same measuring words for listening (எனைத்தானும் ... அனைத்தானும்) but its result is not small: that much too gives full greatness (ஆன்ற பெருமை தரும்). Where 396 states a strict proportion, 416 encourages the listener who can manage only a little; Parimelazhagar draws that moral, that it should not be scorned as small.

417 says those whose wide listening rests on their own close inquiry (இழைத்துணர்ந்து ஈண்டிய கேள்வியவர்) do not speak folly even when they have misunderstood (பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் பேதைமை சொல்லார்). 199 says those of stainless vision, free of delusion (மருள்தீர்ந்த மாசறு காட்சியவர்), do not say empty things even in forgetfulness (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லார்). The two verses have the same shape, a kind of person whose speech stays sound even when the mind lapses, and they credit it to different sources: listening in one, clear vision in the other.

417 says well-grounded listeners do not speak folly even when they have misunderstood (பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும்). 139 says that for those who have conduct, speaking evil even by a slip (வழுக்கியும்) is not possible. The same guarantee, speech that holds even under error, is attached to listening in the Book of Wealth and to conduct in the Book of Virtue.

418 says ears that have not been pierced by listening (கேள்வியால் தோட்கப்படாத செவி) are of the deaf kind even though they hear (கேட்பினுங் கேளாத் தகையவே). 393, in the chapter on learning, says only the learned are said to have eyes, and the unlearned have two sores on the face (முகத்திரண்டு புண்ணுடையர்). The neighbouring chapters make the same move with two organs: the eye that has not learned is not an eye, and the ear that has not listened is not an ear.

418 says an ear unopened by listening does not really hear. 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities is without worth, like a sense organ that does not grasp its object (கோளில் பொறியின் குணமிலவே). Both verses judge a part of the body by whether it does its proper work, and 9 uses the dead sense organ, which is 418's subject, as its comparison.

418 denies real hearing to ears that listening has not opened. 577 says those without kindly regard have no eyes (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர்), and those who have eyes do not lack it. The form of argument is the same, an organ is counted as present only when it is used for its higher purpose, applied to instruction in 418 and to kindness in 577.

419 says it is hard for those without fine listening (நுணங்கிய கேள்வியரல்லார்) to have a mouth that bows (வணங்கிய வாயினர்). 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை), while smallness decks itself out in self-admiration (தன்னை வியந்து). Parimelazhagar's comment on 419, that those who have not listened will speak in admiration of themselves, is 978's picture of smallness; 419 adds where the difference comes from.

419 says humble speech is hardly to be had without fine listening. 844 defines வெண்மை, shallowness of understanding, as the conceit that says 'we have brightness' (ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு). The pair links lack of instruction and self-praise from both ends: 419 says the uninstructed will not speak humbly, and 844 says boasting of one's understanding is itself the mark of lacking it.

95 says being humble and sweet-spoken (பணிவுடையன் இன்சொலன் ஆதல்) is a person's ornament, and nothing else is. 419 says a mouth that bows (வணங்கிய வாய்) is hard to come by without fine listening. 95 holds humble speech up for everyone, and 419 adds a condition: it has to be prepared for by listening.

420 asks what it matters whether they die or live, those மாக்கள் who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear. 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for all living beings (ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல), and the distinction of மாந்தர் is having shame. Both verses treat eating as what humans share with every creature and put human worth elsewhere, in the ear's taste for one and in shame for the other.

406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are otherwise like saline ground that yields nothing (பயவாக் களர்). 420 says of those who have no taste for what the ear takes in that their dying or living makes no difference (அவியினும் வாழினும் என்). The chapters on not learning and on listening reach the same verdict, a life that merely exists; Manakkudavar reads 420, as Parimelazhagar reads 406, as about being of no use to others.

420 treats those without the ear's taste as people whose death and life are the same. 214 says only one who knows what is fitting truly lives (உயிர்வாழ்வான்), and anyone else is counted among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). The book repeatedly denies real life to those who lack one defining quality; here the quality is listening, and in 214 it is knowing one's duty to others.

421 calls understanding an inner fortress that enemies cannot destroy (செறுவார்க்கும் உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண்). 534 says those who have fear have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை); Parimelazhagar explains that forts of forest and hill are of no use to a frightened mind. 534 shows from the negative side why 421 puts the fortress inside: walls protect only as far as the mind behind them holds.

747 says a fort is what is hard to take by encirclement, by assault, or by அறைப்படுத்தல், which Parimelazhagar explains as working on those inside so that it is opened. 421 calls understanding an அரண் that enemies cannot destroy from within (உள்ளழிக்கலாகா); Parimelazhagar allows both 'an inner fort' and 'a fort that cannot be entered and destroyed'. The weak point of a real fort in 747, subversion from inside, is the very thing 421 says understanding is proof against.

421 names understanding as the tool that guards against ruin (அற்றங் காக்குங் கருவி). 781 asks what guard is as hard for hostile action to get past as friendship (வினைக்கரிய யாவுள காப்பு). The Book of Wealth offers two protections that are not walls or weapons, one within the person and one between persons, and praises each in the vocabulary of defence.

422 says understanding does not let one go wherever the mind has gone, but draws away from evil and directs toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). 787 says friendship removes one from what ruins and sets one on the path (அழிவினவை நீக்கி ஆறுய்த்து). The two verses use the same pair of actions and the same verb of steering (உய்); what understanding does for a person from inside, the friend does from outside.

24 says one who guards the five with the goad called firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்) is a seed for the highest ground; the goad makes the senses elephants, as Parimelazhagar spells out. 422 gives understanding a similar job, not letting one go where one has gone (சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா), which Parimelazhagar explains with a rider directing a horse. 422 goes a step past 24's holding back: it also sorts good from evil and steers toward the good.

423 and 355 are built on one frame. 355, on perceiving reality, says: whatever a thing is and of whatever nature (எப்பொருள் எத்தன்மைத்தாயினும்), understanding is seeing the true thing in it (அப்பொருள் மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு). 423 keeps the frame and changes the middle to 'from whoever's mouth it is heard' (யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும்). The same definition of understanding, looking through the appearance to what is true, is applied to things in the Book of Virtue and to reports in the Book of Wealth.

415 praises a particular source, the words from the mouth of those with conduct (ஒழுக்கமுடையார் வாய்ச்சொல்), and Parimelazhagar infers there that the words of those without conduct should not be listened to. 423 says understanding finds the truth in a thing from whoever's mouth it is heard (யார்யார்வாய்), and Parimelazhagar says there that one weighs the matter and not the nature of the speaker. The verses do not contradict each other, but 423 limits how far 415's preference for good speakers can serve as a test of what is true.

423 says understanding sees the true substance of what is said, whoever says it. 1046 observes that even when the poor speak of good matters with full understanding (நற்பொருள் நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லினும்), their words lose their force (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வுபடும்). 1046 describes hearers doing what 423 rules out, judging words by the speaker, and so shows what the standard in 423 is set against.

424 defines understanding in two halves: saying things so that they are easy to grasp and go home (எண்பொருளவாகச் செலச்சொல்லி), and seeing the subtle meaning in what comes from others (பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள் காண்பது). 646, on skill in speech, has the same two halves: speaking so that others want it (வேட்பத்தாஞ் சொல்லி) and taking the benefit of what others say (பிறர்சொல் பயன்கோடல்). The chapters on understanding and on eloquence each treat speaking and listening as one competence.

424 makes it part of understanding to put things so that hearers take them in easily. 650 says those who cannot lay out what they have learned so that others understand (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like a cluster of flowers in bloom with no scent. 650 gives the failure case of 424's first half: learning that cannot be conveyed is counted as lacking something essential. The first word of 650 is misprinted in this edition, though the image is clear from the commentary.

424 says understanding sees the fine meaning in what others say (பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள்); Manakkudavar takes this as seeing what they mean without their spelling it out. 701 praises one who knows what is intended by looking, without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்). 701 carries the second half of 424 one step further, from reading what lies within words to reading what is never put into words.

425 says understanding is what has neither opening nor closing (மலர்தலும் கூம்பலும் இல்லது), which Parimelazhagar reads as steadiness in friendship with the high-minded, unlike a pond flower that opens and shuts. 782 says the friendship of the wise fills like the crescent moon and that of fools shrinks like the moon after full. Both verses judge attachment by a natural cycle; 782 praises the bond that grows, while 425 asks for one that does not swing in either direction.

115 says loss and increase are not absent from life, and that not bending in the heart (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. Parimelazhagar records a second reading of 425, in which the opening and closing are expanding in wealth and shrinking in want. On that reading the two verses say the same thing, that a person should stay the same through gain and loss, one under the heading of fairness and the other of understanding.

425 says embracing the world is brightness (உலகம் தழீஇயது ஒட்பம்). 544 uses the same verb twice: the world stands embracing the feet (அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு) of the king who rules embracing his people (குடிதழீஇ). In 544 the embrace is returned, which gives a concrete reason why 425 counts drawing the world close as intelligence. Parimelazhagar narrows 'the world' in 425 to the high-minded.

426 defines understanding as living with the world in the way the world lives (உலகத்தோடு அவ்வதுறைவது அறிவு). 140 states the converse with the same phrase: those who have not learned to conduct themselves in step with the world (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்), though they have learned much, are without understanding (அறிவிலாதார்). The claim appears once under conduct and once under understanding; Parimelazhagar glosses 'the world' in 140 as the conduct of the high-minded.

426 makes accord with the world part of what understanding is. 850 says one who says 'it is not' of what the world says is (உலகத்தார் உண்டென்பது இல்லென்பான்) will be set down as a demon on earth. 850, in the chapter on shallow understanding, extends 426 from conduct to belief and states the cost of breaking with the world's view.

426 says understanding lives as the world lives. 637 tells the minister that even after knowing the method of doing a thing (செயற்கை அறிந்தக் கடைத்தும்), he should act knowing the way of the world (உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்). The same deference to how the world actually goes is asked of the person of understanding in general and of the expert in statecraft in particular, where it is placed above book method.

427 defines those with understanding as those who know what is going to be (ஆவதறிவார்). 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is ahead (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that comes to shake them. 429 gives the use of the foresight that 427 only defines: knowing beforehand matters because it lets one guard beforehand.

427 separates the wise from the unwise by whether they know what will be (ஆவது). 461 tells one to act after weighing what will be lost, what will come of it (ஆவதூஉம்), and the gain that follows later. 461 turns the foresight of 427 into a procedure, a reckoning of outcomes made before acting.

427 makes knowing what is to come the mark of having understanding, as if it were a trait of the person. 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish (பேதைப்படுக்கும் இழவூழ்) and a fate of gain, when it arrives, widens understanding (அறிவகற்றும் ஆகலூழ்). Read with 372, the division in 427 is not fixed: the same person may see ahead or fail to, depending on what fate is at work.

382 lists fearlessness (அஞ்சாமை) first among the four qualities a king must never lack. 428 says not fearing what is to be feared (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை) is folly, and fearing it is the work of the knowing. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both note the relation at 428: fearlessness has been named a royal excellence, and this verse marks where fear is still required.

201 says those given to evil deeds do not fear the intoxication called evil deed, and the excellent do fear it (தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்). 428 has the same two-sided form: folly does not fear what is to be feared, and the knowing do. 201 supplies an object for 428's unnamed 'what is to be feared'; Parimelazhagar lists sin, blame and ruin there.

428 makes fear of the right things the work of the knowing (அறிவார் தொழில்). 1075 says fear is the whole basis of proper behaviour among the base (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), which Parimelazhagar takes as fear of harm from the king. Together they show that fear in itself does not separate the wise from the low; what separates them is that the wise fear what deserves it and the base behave only for fear of being punished.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is ahead have no affliction that comes to shake them (அதிர வருவதோர் நோய்). 435 says the life of one who does not guard before it comes (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like a straw-heap before fire. They are the positive and negative statements of one rule; 435 stands in the chapter on faults, where Parimelazhagar supplies 'fault' as what comes, while 429 speaks of harm in general.

429 says no shaking affliction comes to those who foresee and guard; Manakkudavar extends this even to suffering due from past deeds, which will not come harshly if guarded against. 380 says nothing is stronger than fate: even if one devises something else, it gets there first (மற்றொன்று சூழினுந் தான்முந்துறும்). The conflict holds if 429 is read as covering every affliction, fated ones included; if 429 is limited to harms that foresight can reach, the two do not collide.

429 credits freedom from shock to an understanding that guards against what is coming. 442 tells a ruler to cherish and keep those who can remove the trouble that has come and guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும் பெற்றியார்). 442 shows that the foresight of 429 need not be the ruler's own: it can be secured by choosing the right people.

430 says those with understanding have everything, and those without it have nothing whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்). 841 says lack of understanding is the lack among lacks (அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை), and the world does not count other lack as lack. 841, opening the chapter on shallow understanding, restates 430 from the side of poverty.

430 defines having by understanding: the wise have all, and the unwise have nothing whatever they own. 591 uses the same turn for energy of mind: it is what makes someone 'one who has' (உடையர் எனப்படுவது ஊக்கம்), and those without it do not really have what they have (உடையது உடையரோ). The book redefines possession in the same words for two different inner qualities.

430 says those with understanding have everything; Parimelazhagar explains that all wealth is made and kept by understanding. 374 says the world's nature is of two separate kinds: having wealth is one thing and being clear-minded is another (திருவேறு தெள்ளியராதலும் வேறு), and Parimelazhagar there raises this very objection, that making and keeping wealth should belong to the wise. The conflict depends on reading 430 as a claim about actual prosperity, as Parimelazhagar does; if 'have everything' means that understanding outweighs possessions, 374 does not contradict it.
